Restatement

You are given n strings S1..Sn, each of length m, over the alphabet {A..Z, .}. Two students i, j are similar if the number of positions t such that Si[t] = Sj[t] ≠ '.' is at least k. Among all similar pairs (a, b) with a < b, you must output the one with the smallest b; if several have the same b, choose the one with the largest a. If there is no similar pair, output -1.

Key observations

- Similarity is exactly the overlap size of the sets Ti = {(t, Si[t]) : Si[t] ≠ '.'} and Tj.
- k ≤ 5 is very small; m ≤ 3000, n ≤ 5000 are large. A naive O(n^2 m) check is too slow.
- Tie-breaking is friendly to a “scan b from 2 to n” approach: the first b where we can find a valid a is the correct smallest b; within that b, we just need the largest a.

A crucial pigeonhole trick when k ≥ 2

Partition the columns by their index modulo P = k − 1 (for k ≥ 2). There are P residue classes, each containing about m/P columns. Take any pair (i, j) whose total number of matches is at least k. Distribute these k matching columns into the P classes; by the pigeonhole principle, at least one residue class contains at least ceil(k/P) = 2 matches (since P = k − 1 and k ≥ 2).

Therefore:
- If two students are similar (≥ k matches overall), then for some residue class r (columns with indices ≡ r mod P), they already match in at least 2 columns.

This gives a necessary condition that is much easier to test fast: “there exists a residue r where i and j match in ≥ 2 columns.” We will use this to generate a small candidate set for a given b and then verify the candidates exactly.

Bitset view (across students)

- For each column j and letter c ∈ {A..Z}, precompute a bitset B[j][c] of length n over students: B[j][c][i] = 1 if and only if Si[j] = c, else 0.
  - Memory: 26·m bitsets of n bits each. With n = 5000, m = 3000, this is ~26·3000·5000 ≈ 3.9e8 bits ≈ 49 MB, which is acceptable.

- For the current right endpoint student b, we only care about previous students, so we will always mask with a prefix mask Prev[b] that has bits 1..b−1 set and b..n zero; hence per b we only touch the first ceil((b−1)/wordsize) machine words of each bitset.

Detecting “≥ 2 matches in a residue” for b in O(number_of_columns_for_b × number_of_words)

Fix b and a residue class r (0 ≤ r < P). Let the multiset Cr(b) = { (j, c) : j ≡ r (mod P) and Sb[j] = c ≠ '.' }. For this r, we want the set of students a < b that appear in at least two of the bitsets {B[j][c] : (j, c) ∈ Cr(b)}.

This can be computed with two accumulator bitsets using a saturating “two-of-many” counter:
- Hit1r: students having matched b at least once in this residue so far;
- Hit2r: students having matched b at least twice in this residue so far.

Process all pairs (j, c) in Cr(b) and update:
- X = Hit1r AND (B[j][c] AND Prev[b])
- Hit2r |= X
- Hit1r |= (B[j][c] AND Prev[b])

After finishing this residue r, Hit2r marks exactly those a < b with at least two matches against b within residue class r. Let Candidate2(b) be the union OR of Hit2r over all residues r. By the pigeonhole lemma, any a that is truly similar to b (≥ k matches overall) must be in Candidate2(b).

Why this is fast:
- Each update uses only a small, constant number of bitwise operations per machine word (just AND and OR).
- For k ≥ 2 there are P = k − 1 residues; total work per b is proportional to the number of columns answered by b times the number of machine words Wb = ceil((b−1)/wordsize). Summed over all b, the number of 64-bit word operations is on the order of 2·m·Σb Wb ≈ 2·m·n^2/128 (wordsize=64). With m=3000, n=5000, this is roughly 1.17e9 primitive bitwise ops, which is feasible in optimized implementations.

Selecting the answer for b

- From Candidate2(b) take all set bits a < b. We must pick the largest a that truly has ≥ k matches with b.
- Verify candidates a in decreasing order of a:
  - Count the exact number of matches between Sa and Sb:
    - Simple and memory-lean approach: scan j from 1..m, increment a counter whenever Sb[j] ≠ '.' and Sa[j] = Sb[j]; break as soon as the counter reaches k.
    - Alternatively (faster if memory allows), precompute for each student i and letter c a bitset Ai[c] over columns (Ai[c][j] = 1 iff Si[j] = c) and compute sum over c popcount(Aa[c] & Ab[c]) with early stop at k.
  - The first a (largest) that reaches ≥ k gives the pair (a, b).
- If no candidate works for this b, continue with b+1.
- The first b that yields a valid pair is the globally minimal b (we scan b in increasing order), and within it we explicitly take the largest a.

k = 1 special case

If k = 1 you only need any single equal answered position. This can be done in O(n·m) without bitsets:
- Maintain for each (j, c) the largest index last[j][c] of a student seen so far having c in column j.
- For b from 2 to n:
  - For all columns j where Sb[j] = c ≠ '.', candidate a := max over last[j][c].
  - If candidate a exists, output (a, b).
  - Then update last[j][c] := b for all such j.

This automatically produces the minimal b and, for that b, the largest possible a.

Putting it all together: algorithm

Preprocessing
- Read the strings S1..Sn.
- Build B[j][c] bitsets over students for all j ∈ [1..m], c ∈ [A..Z].
- Optionally (for faster verification) also build Ai[c] bitsets over columns for all students i and c (this mirrors B and costs similar memory). If you’d rather save memory, verify by scanning characters of Sa and Sb directly.

Main loop
- If k = 1: use the simple O(n·m) approach above and return as soon as you find a pair; if none, print -1.
- Else (k ≥ 2):
  - P := k − 1.
  - For b from 2 to n:
    - Candidate := empty bitset over students.
    - For r in 0..P−1:
      - Hit1 := 0, Hit2 := 0.
      - For columns j ≡ r (mod P):
        - If Sb[j] = c ≠ '.':
          - Bj := B[j][c] masked to indices < b (only the first Wb words).
          - X := Hit1 & Bj
          - Hit2 |= X
          - Hit1 |= Bj
      - Candidate |= Hit2
    - If Candidate has any bit set:
      - For a from b−1 down to 1:
        - If Candidate[a] = 1:
          - Verify whether (a, b) truly has ≥ k matches:
            - Either via a simple scan over columns (early-breaking at k),
            - Or via bitset intersections per letter (early-breaking).
          - If true, print a b and stop the program.
  - If the loop finishes without finding a pair, print -1.

Correctness proof

- Soundness of candidate generation: Suppose (a, b) is a similar pair with at least k matching answered columns. Partition those k columns by their residues modulo P = k − 1. At least one residue class contains at least 2 of these columns (pigeonhole). When we process b and this residue, both those columns j1, j2 contribute Bj1 and Bj2 containing bit a; the incremental update will:
  - Set a in Hit1 after the first such column,
  - Then, upon processing the second, a will be added to Hit2 via X = Hit1 & Bj.
  Thus a ∈ Candidate2(b).
- Completeness for the final answer: We scan b in increasing order; the first time we find a valid pair (a, b), this b is minimal. For that b, we check candidates a in decreasing order, so the first verified a is the largest with ≥ k matches. Therefore, the output obeys the required tie-breaking.

Complexity and limits

- Preprocessing: O(n·m) time, ~50 MB memory for B; optionally another ~50 MB for Ai if you choose the bitset-based verification.
- Main loop (k ≥ 2):
  - Candidate construction per b: Sum over residues and columns answered by b of a small constant number of bitwise ops per word. Summed over b, this is roughly 2·m·Σb ceil((b−1)/64) ≈ 2·m·n^2/128 operations. With n=5000, m=3000 this is about 1.17e9 primitive operations. These are simple AND/OR on 64-bit words and fit in 3 seconds in an optimized implementation.
  - Verification: In practice few candidates need exact checking. Each check costs O(m) simple comparisons with early stop at k, or O(26·(m/wordsize)) with the letter-bitset approach.
- k = 1: O(n·m) straightforward.

Implementation tips

- Store bitsets as flat arrays of 64-bit words; avoid high-overhead dynamic bitset abstractions inside tight loops.
- For b, only iterate the first Wb words (Wb = ceil((b−1)/64)): future students are irrelevant.
- Build per-residue the list of columns once so you don’t recompute j ≡ r repeatedly.
- Verification fast path: before the exact count, compute a trivial upper bound ub = sum over c min(count of c in Sa, count of c in Sb). If ub < k, skip this candidate immediately. Precompute per-student letter counts once; this costs almost nothing and prunes many candidates.

Pseudocode sketch (k ≥ 2)

- Precompute:
  - For each j in [1..m], each c in [A..Z]: bitset B[j][c] over students.
  - For each residue r: cols_r = [j : 1 ≤ j ≤ m and j % (k-1) == r].

- For b = 2..n:
  - Candidate := zeros(n)
  - Wb := ceil((b-1)/64)
  - For r = 0..k-2:
    - Hit1 := zeros(n), Hit2 := zeros(n)
    - For j in cols_r:
      - c := Sb[j]; if c == '.' continue
      - Bj := prefix_mask(B[j][c], Wb)
      - X := Hit1[0..Wb-1] & Bj[0..Wb-1]
      - Hit2[0..Wb-1] |= X
      - Hit1[0..Wb-1] |= Bj[0..Wb-1]
    - Candidate[0..Wb-1] |= Hit2[0..Wb-1]
  - For a = b-1 down to 1:
    - If Candidate[a] == 0: continue
    - If verify(Sa, Sb, k) == true:
      - print a, b; return
- print -1

Verification verify(Sa, Sb, k):
- cnt := 0
- For j = 1..m:
  - if Sb[j] != '.' and Sa[j] == Sb[j]:
    - cnt++; if cnt == k return true
- return false

Why it fits and works

- The candidate generation step uses the strong necessary condition (≥ 2 matches within a residue class) derived from a tight pigeonhole bound for k ≤ 5. It is both correct and exceptionally amenable to fast bit-parallel implementation.
- The time is dominated by a large but simple number of 64-bit AND/OR operations, with good cache behavior (we always scan contiguous words).
- The tie-break is handled naturally by scanning b increasing and testing a decreasing.
- Memory stays within reasonable bounds and can be halved if you verify by character scans instead of letter-bitsets.

This approach is robust, exact (no false negatives or positives in the final decision), adheres to the time and memory limits, and handles all edge cases (including many dots, all-equal strings, and adversarial distributions).
